CausalChain: m6A modification of lncRNAs -> Altered lncRNA secondary structure -> Increased binding affinity to RNA-binding proteins -> Stabilization of mRNAs for metabolic enzymes and cytokines -> Metabolic reprogramming (e.g., enhanced glycolysis) and upregulation of immunosuppressive factors -> Formation of an immunosuppressive liver microenvironment -> Promotion of HCC progression
Hypothesis: m6A-induced structural alterations in lncRNAs foster enhanced interactions with RNA-binding proteins that stabilize mRNAs governing metabolism and immune regulation, thereby simultaneously promoting metabolic reprogramming and an immunosuppressive microenvironment that drive hepatocellular carcinoma progression.
Abstract: In this study, we hypothesize that m6A modifications on specific long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) reprogram their secondary structures, thereby enhancing their interaction with RNA-binding proteins. This enhanced binding leads to the stabilization of mRNAs encoding critical metabolic enzymes and immunomodulatory factors, which in turn drives both metabolic reprogramming (such as elevated glycolysis) and the emergence of an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). These dual influences may cooperatively fuel HCC progression and resistance to conventional therapies. Targeting either the m6A modification process or the interactions between modified lncRNAs and their binding partners might provide novel therapeutic avenues for HCC.
